notes: TBox rule edit. No real exceptions: criterion 6 of the Open Source Definition forbids any OSI-approved license from restricting use in a business, so every approved license (MIT, GPL, Apache, MPL, ...) permits commercial use. Different from technology-0006 (GPL programs are free software): this rule is about the OSI's approved class and a use permission. The MIT License is the well-known member: OSI approval is an institutional listing, so in w1 it can leave the approved class without breaking firm facts outside the chain (it stays a permissive license; other licenses keep their own status). Larchmont, Quarrel and Fennick are invented, so the rule is their only route. The near query's answer (the OSI) differs from the new answer (no) and does not follow from the edit; Rule 1: 'commercial use' covers selling and running paid services, which every OSI license allows, copyleft included. Side facts of the edit itself (every world): OSI approval means meeting the Open Source Definition, so its criterion 6 and the belief 'open-source licenses permit commercial use' (and 'permissive licenses permit proprietary use', for OSI-approved permissive licenses) change with the rule; otherwise Larchmont and Fennick would get a second route. The commercial use of GPL, Apache or MIT code by companies is contradicted by the edit in every world (GPL and Apache are members too), so it does not rule out w2; the MIT text's 'sell copies' clause is the member's own property, which is what gives way in w2, not a fact outside the chain. Rule 1 edge cases checked: Artistic License 1.0 bars charging a fee for the Package itself but allows use in business and commercial aggregate distribution; NPOSL-3.0's 'non-profit' is about the licensor, and its grant has no field-of-use limit. No OSI-approved license forbids commercial use.
